meta_description: Software companies are instrumented but not decisioned: events arrive, dashboards exist, and monetization, trust, and cost decisions still run on exports. Dataq Software builds the revenue-data spine — events to metering to rating to recognition — plus trust evidence automation and unit economics that survive scale.

blocks.x: A modern software company emits more decision-grade data than most banks it sells to — every click, API call, model token, and background job, every deployment, every hourly cloud cost line — and still runs pricing, revenue recognition, audit preparation, and margin reviews on exports and instinct. The gap is not instrumentation; it is the decision layer that was never built on top of it. Dataq Software builds that layer: a revenue-data spine from event to meter to invoice to recognized revenue, trust evidence automation that survives auditor season, and unit economics computed on your own telemetry.

A Series-C software company with a usage-based product ships more instrumentation than most banks it pitches. Every click, API call, model token, and background job emits an event; every deploy emits logs and traces; every cloud account emits an hourly cost line. Yet the pricing committee argues from anecdote, finance reconstructs revenue recognition in workbooks at quarter close, and the security team spends three weeks per enterprise questionnaire copy-pasting from last year's answers. The instrumentation is not the problem. The decision layer that should sit on top of it was never built, so the most expensive decisions in the company run on exports.

The vocabulary of that gap is familiar to every software executive. Product-qualified leads never reach sales because scoring runs on a stale weekly export. Net revenue retention gets quoted as one number when the decomposition — expansion by seat, expansion by usage, contraction, gross churn — is what the board actually needs. ASC 606 questions on consumption revenue get answered with ad-hoc queries engineering resents. Cloud cost per tenant cannot be allocated because tagging was optional two years ago, and the AI feature nobody priced by token is now a third of cost of goods sold. Each of these is a data engineering problem wearing a business-process costume.

Dataq Software works as an engineering partner on the estate you already run — your event pipeline, your billing ledger, your warehouse, your cloud accounts, your CI/CD. We do not replace the CRM, the ERP, or the data platform; we build the semantic and decision layers that make them answer monetization, trust, and margin questions at operating speed. Engagements start with a two-week baseline against your own data, and carry an honest stop condition: if the instrumentation cannot support the decision, the baseline report says what to instrument before any pipeline is worth building.
Instrumented but not decisioned: the missing decision layer

The symptoms are consistent across growth-stage software companies. Dashboards exist for everything and decide nothing: the weekly metrics review reads charts, then makes its real calls on instinct. Ownership is split so finely that no team owns a decision end to end — product owns events, finance owns revenue, platform owns cloud cost, security owns trust, and the joins between them are weekly meetings and spreadsheets. The result is decision latency that compounds: pricing changes take a quarter of analysis, the SOC 2 audit eats six weeks of engineering time, and the board deck's NRR number arrives with a footnote explaining why it disagrees with the billing system.

The alternative is not another dashboard. It is a decision layer with named objects and owners: a metering pipeline that is the system of record for what counts; a rating and recognition path that turns usage into invoices and journal entries; a tenant-level cost allocation that survives a FinOps audit; an evidence pipeline that produces audit artifacts continuously instead of annually. Software companies built ingestion because engineers like instruments. Building the layer after ingestion is a different discipline — schema contracts, revenue semantics, control evidence — and it is the one this page describes.

None of these failures comes from missing tools. The warehouse has the data, the dashboards render it, and the meetings happen on schedule. What is missing is decision infrastructure: named objects with owners, latency targets, and audit trails — meters that finance trusts, entitlements the gateway enforces, allocations the board can read, evidence an auditor samples directly. That is a build, not a procurement, which is why software companies with excellent tooling still run their most expensive decisions on exports and instinct. Every company at this stage has the tools; almost none has the connective decisions built on top of them.
Event ingestion and schema governance: the contract under everything

Product analytics starts as a happy heap: every team ships events, naming conventions drift, and two years later nobody can safely change an event schema because three dashboards, a churn model, and the billing prototype all read it. The heap is the reason activation funnels disagree with each other and with the billing ledger. Event schema governance — a registry, versioned contracts, deprecation windows, automated checks in CI — is unglamorous and decisive: it is what makes downstream monetization and retention models trustworthy, because their inputs stop changing under them.

We build ingestion with the same discipline as a public API: documented contracts, compatibility rules, and a test that fails the build when an event breaks its schema. Identity resolution gets explicit treatment — anonymous-to-known stitching, account hierarchies, the workspace-versus-user distinction that seat-versus-usage pricing depends on. The output is an event stream the rest of the stack can build on: deduplicated, ordered, enriched with tenant and plan context, and versioned well enough that a schema change ships with a migration note rather than a broken funnel. Downstream consumers subscribe to contracts instead of to whatever arrived that week.

Governance is also the cheapest work on this page to do early. A schema registry costs weeks before scale and saves quarters after it; the same holds for identity-resolution conventions and the tenant-versus-user distinction. Companies that skip it rebuild funnels every two years and relitigate whose numbers are right in every growth review; companies that do it early spend their analytics effort on decisions instead of repair. The deliverable is small by design — contracts, checks in CI, and a migration note per change. It is the rare investment that gets cheaper the earlier it lands.
Activation funnels and cohort retention that product reviews weekly

Activation and retention are the two numbers a product-led company lives by, and both fail quietly when the event layer is a heap. Activation needs an agreed definition — not a dashboard argument but a versioned specification: which events, within what window, for which persona, counted against which cohort entry. Without the specification, every team optimizes a different funnel and the weekly review arbitrates definitions instead of decisions. Retention needs cohort logic that matches how the business actually sells: by account, by workspace, by seat, not by an anonymous device identifier that resets every time a browser clears cookies.

We build both as datasets with definitions in code, so the funnel the growth team reviews is the same one the churn model trains on and the same one finance quotes when expansion revenue is attributed. Cohort retention decomposes into the segments that drive action — plan, channel, onboarding variant, account size — and lands in the operating review as a table, not a screenshot. The practical test of a working funnel layer is boring: when someone changes the activation definition, the system shows who approved it, what changed downstream, and which historical comparisons are no longer apples-to-apples.
NRR decomposition: seat versus usage, expansion versus drift

Net revenue retention is the number boards quote and the number least often decomposed honestly. Expansion gets booked in aggregate when its composition matters: seats added by existing accounts versus usage uplift versus plan upgrades versus price increases — four different motions with different durability, different cost to serve, and different signals about product-market fit. Contraction hides inside the same aggregate: seats removed at annual renewals, usage fading on a feature nobody promoted, discounting that books as flat NRR while eroding unit economics. The aggregate is not wrong; it is insufficient for any decision it is quoted to support.

We build NRR as a decomposed dataset on the billing ledger and the metering pipeline: every account's month-over-month movement attributed to seat change, usage change, plan change, discount change, or churn, with cohort views by segment, entry motion, and contract term. The decomposition feeds the operating review and the board deck from the same source, and it feeds sales: an account whose usage is flat while seats grow is a different conversation from one whose usage is decaying at renewal. When pricing changes, the decomposition shows which motion actually moved, which is the only honest way to price again.

The decomposition also disciplines the roadmap. Expansion attributed to usage on one surface, contraction concentrated on another, and churn clustered in one onboarding cohort are roadmap signals wearing revenue clothes — and they arrive weekly instead of quarterly once the spine exists. The same table prices honesty: a pricing change that lifts booked expansion while usage per seat falls is visible within one cohort cycle, before the comp plan pays out on it. When the board asks what is driving NRR, the answer is a query with attribution, not a narrative assembled the night before.
Metering pipelines and entitlements: the system of record for what counts

Metering is where monetization lives or dies, and most companies discover its importance during the first enterprise contract dispute. What counts as a unit — a successful API call or every attempt? When is it counted — at request, at completion, at month close? Who gets the benefit of a retry? Metering is a distributed-systems problem with revenue consequences: exactly-once delivery is expensive, at-least-once needs idempotent aggregation, and late-arriving events need a policy, not a shrug. Entitlements ride the same pipeline: what a plan allows, what an override grants, what a sales-led pilot promises the API will enforce.

We build metering as an append-only event path with idempotent aggregation into billable periods, late-data windows tuned to the product, and reconciliation reports that explain any variance between raw events and billed units. Entitlement state lives beside it, versioned per tenant per plan, consumed by the API gateway at request time and auditable at dispute time. The deliverable that changes executive behavior is the reconciliation view: raw events, aggregated meters, rated amounts, and invoiced amounts side by side, so the question of why a tenant's bill doubled has a query instead of a war room.

Metering is the only subsystem in this stack whose bugs are discovered by customers holding invoices. Its design standard is audit-grade, not analytics-grade — idempotent, reconcilable, and traceable to raw events.
Usage-based billing, rating, and ASC 606 on consumption

Usage-based rating looks like arithmetic until contract terms arrive: tiered with breakpoints, volume commits with draw-down order, minimums with true-ups, prepaid credits with expiries, overages capped or uncapped. Then revenue recognition adds its own semantics — ASC 606 treats usage revenue differently depending on whether it is a usage-based royalty-style right, a series, or a stand-ready obligation — and the sales quota, the invoice, and the journal entry must all agree on which interpretation applies. Spreadsheets survive this for a while, at the cost of a close that engineering supports with ad-hoc queries.

We build rating as a versioned rules engine over metered aggregates, with contract terms as data — commit balances, draw-down order, credit expiries, caps — and every invoice traceable to the meters and rules that produced it. Revenue recognition runs on the same spine: usage recognized as delivered or ratably, overage timing treated consistently, contract modifications handled as amendments rather than mysteries. The quarter-close artifact becomes a report with drill-down to the underlying events, which converts the finance team from a requester of ad-hoc queries into an owner of a system. When auditors ask how usage revenue is computed, the answer is a documented path, not a person.

The distinction that matters operationally is between rating and recognition as one system versus two coupled ones. Rating answers what the customer owes; recognition answers when the company may book it; the contract answers both from the same terms. Companies that fuse them into one pipeline break every time a revenue-policy interpretation changes; companies that keep them separate with shared terms data survive policy changes and auditor questions without re-engineering billing. We build them separate and joined — one terms source, two deterministic consumers. Auditors read that separation favorably, and engineering stops relitigating revenue policy inside billing code.
Feature flags, rollouts, and experimentation discipline

Feature flags begin as release engineering and end as governance. Left untended, a codebase accumulates thousands of dormant flags nobody can safely delete, experiments run without power calculations, and rollouts ship to ten percent of traffic for months because nobody owned the promotion decision. The cost is real: flags add branching to code, experiments add noise to the metrics every other team reads, and stale flags have caused outages at companies with far larger platform teams than yours. The governance gap stays invisible until an incident forces an inventory of who can flip what in production, and by then the inventory itself takes days.

We build the flag and experiment layer as governed infrastructure: a registry with owners and expiry dates, rollout policies tied to SLOs so a flagged feature auto-halts when its error budget burns, and experiment pipelines that compute power before launch and read from the same event contracts as the retention models. Results land in the operating review with the metrics that matter — activation impact, retention impact, performance cost — and the promotion-or-rollback decision gets an owner and a date. The point is not more experiments; it is fewer, decided faster, with evidence the whole company can read.
SLOs, error budgets, and incident command

Reliability decisions need a currency, and the industry's currency is the SLO and its error budget. What breaks most SaaS programs is not the math — it is the disconnect between the SLO dashboard and the decisions: reliability goals nobody derived from customer contracts, error budgets that burn without triggering any behavior change, incidents whose postmortems produce action items nobody tracks to closure. The artifact that fixes this is boring and decisive: a service catalog mapping each customer-facing surface to its SLO, its budget policy, and the alerts that page a human.

We help platform teams make that catalog real: SLOs derived from contract terms and support escalation history, error-budget policies wired into release gating, incident command roles rehearsed, and blameless postmortems with tracked follow-through. The measure of maturity is not zero incidents — it is decision speed: how long between a budget breach and a scope decision, how long between an incident and a postmortem with owners. Support data joins the loop, because ticket volume by feature is the demand-side signal that tells you which reliability investment customers would actually notice.
Release engineering and the API as a product

For a software company, the API is often the product, and it deserves the same monetization and experience discipline as any SKU. Rate limits are pricing. API analytics are product analytics. SDK adoption is activation. Developer experience is onboarding. Companies that treat these as engineering details leave revenue and retention on the table: the endpoint with rising latency and rising call volume is a churn signal nobody routed; the API pattern customers want and the SDK makes painful is a support cost nobody attributed. The discipline is familiar; applying it to the API surface is what most platform teams have never been staffed or asked to do.

We build the API-product layer on the same spine as everything else: per-tenant usage by endpoint, latency distributions against SLOs, rate-limit behavior as entitlement data, SDK adoption funnels from install to first successful call. CI/CD and release engineering get the same treatment — release trains, canary policies, change failure rates — because the release process is where the error budget is spent. The combined view answers the questions growth reviews skip: which API surface drives the usage your pricing monetizes, which drives the support load your margin absorbs, and which release changed either.

API productization also changes how deprecation happens. Versioned endpoints with usage-by-tenant views let you retire old surfaces with evidence: who still calls v1, how much, on which plans, and what the migration path costs them. The alternative — breaking changes discovered in support tickets — taxes both trust and the error budget. Rate-limit overrides become entitlement data with owners, so a promise made in a negotiation is enforced by the gateway instead of remembered by a chat channel, and SDK releases carry the same adoption funnels and version-skew visibility as any product surface.
Trust evidence automation: SOC 2, ISO 27001, and the questionnaire queue

SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 are evidence businesses: auditors do not certify intentions, they sample controls and ask for proof that the controls operated over the period. In most companies the proof is assembled by hand — screenshots of access reviews, exports of ticket queues, HR rosters pasted into control matrices — for six weeks before fieldwork, then repeated for every enterprise questionnaire that arrives in the same quarter. Every missing artifact becomes an engineer's week, and the same engineers are the ones the audit is supposed to protect from exactly that work. The evidence exists in systems: IAM, HRIS, ticketing, CI/CD, cloud logs. It is the assembly that is manual.

We build evidence automation on your systems: continuous collection of the artifacts controls require — access review outputs, joiner-mover-leaver records, vulnerability scan summaries, change tickets, backup verification — mapped to control references and retained with timestamps. Trust center workflows absorb the questionnaire volume: reusable control answers with named owners, evidence links, and version history, so vendor risk questionnaires become an assembly task instead of an engineering detour. The audit changes shape too, because continuous evidence with timestamps is stronger than artifacts reconstructed at fieldwork, and your auditor's sampling approach is tested against the pipeline before the window opens.
Data residency, GDPR, and the residency query

Data residency and GDPR commitments are architecture facts, and they deserve a queryable answer: which tenants store data in which regions, which sub-processors touch it, what the deletion path is, and where cross-border processing occurs. We model residency as data about deployment topology, joined to the trust evidence layer, so the DPA answer, the questionnaire answer, and the auditor answer are the same query. When a prospect in a new region asks where their data lives, the answer is demonstrated rather than asserted — and when a sub-processor changes, the affected-tenant list is computed, not recalled from memory.
Cloud unit economics: COGS per tenant and the AI token question

Gross margin per account is the number SaaS boards rarely see and most need. Computing it honestly requires joining cloud spend to tenants, which requires tagging that was enforced years earlier and a cost model that handles shared services without pretending every tenant pays the same share of the Kubernetes bill. Usage-based products sharpen the problem: AI features convert inference tokens directly into cost of goods sold, and a single tenant's embedding job can move a segment's margin. Without allocation, pricing decisions for those features are guesses with dashboards attached. The pricing question is therefore an allocation question first, and allocation is a data problem, not a spreadsheet season.

We build unit-economics systems on existing cloud billing: enforced tagging and a fallback allocation model for the untaggable, COGS per tenant and per segment recomputed on a schedule finance trusts, and margin decomposition that separates platform fixed cost from tenant-variable cost. AI features get their own ledger — tokens per tenant per feature per model — joined to the rating pipeline so pricing experiments can price tokens against observed consumption instead of intuition. The output that matters is comparative: gross margin by segment, by plan, by tenant cohort, moving quarter over quarter, with the drivers attributed rather than averaged away.
Support-to-product loops: tickets per account and friction telemetry

Support is the highest-signal, worst-joined dataset in most software companies. Tickets know which accounts are struggling, which features generate friction, which onboarding paths fail, and which defect classes recur — and almost none of that reaches product prioritization or churn models, because the ticket system is not joined to the account, plan, and usage data that gives it meaning. The symptoms show up as support-driven churn discovered at the exit interview and as product decisions argued from the loudest customer rather than the pattern. The system of record for customer pain is structurally walled off from the system of record for customer value.

We build the join: tickets per account normalized against usage and tenure, friction telemetry that links support volume to the features involved, and escalation paths that carry product context with the ticket. The churn model gains its strongest early features — ticket trajectory, first-response times, unresolved severity mix — and product review gains a demand-side table: features ranked by tickets per active tenant, weighted by account value. Support stops being a cost center that reports queue length and becomes an input to the roadmap with evidence attached. Which feature counts as friction comes from the data, not from the loudest renewal call.

The loop also runs the other way: product telemetry predicts support load. Deploys that correlate with ticket spikes, features whose adoption outpaces their documentation, tenants whose usage pattern precedes an escalation — all computable once ticketing joins the spine. The metric that changes executive behavior is tickets per active tenant weighted by account value, trending by feature: the demand side of the roadmap, computed rather than asserted. Support leadership gets defensible staffing models instead of queue-length folklore, and the escalation path arrives with product context attached, which shortens resolution and removes the tell-us-what-you-already-typed ritual customers hate. None of this changes how support works day to day; it changes what the work is allowed to inform.
Pricing, packaging, and PLG experiments that produce decisions

Pricing is the highest-leverage decision in software and the least instrumented. Packaging experiments run rarely because revenue systems make them expensive: entitlements hardcoded, rating rules coupled to plan codes, finance unable to model a tier change without engineering support. Product-led motions suffer the same coupling — product-qualified lead scoring runs on a stale export, so the accounts showing expansion behavior in usage data arrive in sales weeks after the signal, at renewal time instead of budget time. The result is a pricing committee that debates in anecdotes and a growth motion whose best leads decay in a queue.

We build pricing and packaging infrastructure that makes experiments cheap: entitlements as data, rating rules versioned and testable against historical meters, quote-to-invoice paths that handle a pilot tier without a fork in the billing system. PQL scoring runs on the live spine — usage intensity, breadth of seats, API adoption, support friction — routed to sales with the evidence attached and timed to budget windows. Every experiment closes the loop: the pricing committee sees revenue per account, gross margin per account, and NRR composition for each cohort that touched the new packaging, which is what makes the next experiment worth running.

Pricing experiments stay cheap only while entitlements, rating, and recognition remain decoupled. The moment a tier hardcodes into three systems, the experiment budget is spent on plumbing instead of learning.
Multi-tenancy and capacity: the architecture behind unit economics

Tenancy architecture is a unit-economics decision wearing a database decision's clothes. Shared-schema multi-tenancy buys density and pays in noisy neighbors and compliance isolation work; siloed tenancy buys isolation and predictability and pays in per-tenant fixed cost that destroys margins at the small end of the customer base. Hybrid estates — shared for the long tail, siloed for regulated enterprise tenants — are the honest answer most platforms eventually reach, and they make both cost allocation and residency commitments strictly data problems. The choice is rarely revisited once made, which is why its data model matters more than its migration.

We model the tenancy topology as data — which tenant runs where, on which shared or dedicated substrate, with which residency and isolation guarantees — and join it to the cost and reliability layers. Capacity planning runs against observed per-tenant load curves and growth trajectories instead of peak-plus-folklore, autoscaling policy reads the same curves, and the COGS-per-tenant model reflects the true substrate each tenant occupies. When a regulated prospect asks where their data lives and how it is isolated, the answer is a query against the topology, which closes enterprise deals and keeps the margin model honest at the same time.
What changes by sector: fintech, gaming, semiconductors

The spine is common across technology companies; the semantics per sector are not. What changes is what the meters mean, what the evidence obligations are, and where unit economics hide. A payments company's transaction pipeline is its metering pipeline and its compliance surface at once. A gaming studio's economy telemetry is both product analytics and fraud surface. A semiconductor or hardware company stretches the same skeleton across long design cycles and component supply. The vocabulary differs; the engineering pattern — ingest, model, decision, evidence — holds across all of them.

items: Fintech and digital natives

Metering is transaction volume with regulator-facing completeness rules; revenue recognition rides payment rails and interchange semantics; trust evidence includes PCI DSS scope statements and financial controls. The revenue-data spine doubles as the reconciliation layer finance already needs at settlement.
Gaming studios

Event ingestion is economy telemetry at enormous volume; cohort retention spans install through day-N engagement; monetization splits between in-app purchase, battle passes, and ad revenue with different recognition timing; capacity planning is launch-day traffic shaped by marketing spend.
Semiconductor and hardware companies

The lifecycle stretches across design cycles, tape-outs, and supply allocation; product analytics becomes device telemetry and field-failure data; unit economics join BOM cost, yield, and wafer starts to per-product margin; trust evidence spans component traceability and export-control documentation.
Vertical SaaS and marketplaces

Two-sided metering — supply utilization and demand activity — drives take-rate economics; NRR decomposition splits marketplace liquidity from subscription seats; trust evidence includes seller verification and content moderation records that enterprise buyers increasingly audit.

blocks.x: How Dataq Software engages

Engagements begin against your own data, in your cloud account, with a baseline that prices the delta before any build is approved. The two-week entry point is standard because it is the shortest interval over which the estate reveals whether its inputs can carry the decisions at hand. Build decisions that follow are gated on what the baseline proves, sized to the joins it exposes, and delivered into your repository with documentation and runbooks your team owns. Nothing in the engagement requires replacing your billing system, CRM, warehouse, or cloud accounts; the work connects them, and the connective tissue is where the decision speed comes from.

blocks.x: Questions technology and SaaS leaders ask us

items: We have a data warehouse and dashboards. Why do decisions still run on exports?

A warehouse stores answers; a decision layer owns objects — meters, entitlements, evidence, allocations — with owners, latency, and auditability. Dashboards built on exported extracts inherit every gap in the extracts; the spine removes the exports and the meetings that reconcile them.
Can you work with our existing billing system?

Yes. Rating and recognition run beside it, fed by metering, with reconciliation views that explain variance. Replacing billing is occasionally the right call; it is never the entry point, and the baseline will say if it is even necessary.
Is SOC 2 evidence automation actually audit-acceptable?

Auditors accept evidence collected continuously from systems of record — it is stronger than screenshots assembled at fieldwork. We map collection to your control matrix and test it against your auditor's sampling approach before the window opens.
How do you handle seat versus usage pricing in one contract?

Contract terms become data: committed seats rate monthly, metered overage draws down against commits in agreed order, and the recognition treatment per component is configured once. The invoice, the quota, and the journal entry read the same terms.
Who owns what you build after the engagement?
You do — code in your repository, pipelines in your cloud account, documentation and runbooks for your team. Dataq Software is hired to close a delta, not to hold the keys.
What about AI feature costs specifically?
Tokens per tenant per feature per model become a ledger joined to rating and to the margin cube, so pricing and margin review see the cost where it occurs instead of averaged into platform COGS.
What if our event data is too messy to build on?

That is a finding, not a failure. The baseline quantifies schema coverage, identity resolution quality, and late-data behavior, and prices the remediation. If the fix is instrumentation rather than a pipeline, the report says so.
We are pre-product-market-fit. Is any of this premature?

The parts that scale with you are cheap to start: schema governance and a tenant graph cost little before scale and save rewrites after it. The parts that need scale have clear triggers — usage-based contracts, enterprise security reviews, AI features on the bill — and the baseline tells you which trigger you are near.

blocks.x: Bring one question your company currently answers with exports — decomposing NRR, reconciling usage to invoices, allocating cloud cost per tenant, or assembling SOC 2 evidence — and one quarter of the relevant data. Dataq Software baselines it in two weeks against your own estate: what the data supports today, where the joins break, and what a decision-grade build would take, priced as a fixed engagement. The deliverable is a scored gap report with the reconciliation views that make the gap visible to your board. If the instrumentation cannot carry the decision, the report says what to instrument, and we stop there rather than sell a pipeline on inputs that cannot hold it.
